headline: New moon springs building off Block Island as the bonito corridor widens toward Newport
subhead: Giant-class bass are still working the Southwest Ledge and North Rip while a collapsed cold wall in Rhode Island Sound opens the door for early bonito east of the Ledge.
body_markdown:
We're coming off a week where the moon was waning down toward new, which meant smaller tidal swings and a slower current at the rips — the kind of stretch where you have to work harder for your bites but the fish that do show are usually quality. That's exactly what played out. The Southwest Ledge fished better on the last two hours of the ebb than on the flood, and the North Rip wanted a slack tide bite instead of the usual full-current push. Water out on the Ledge has held clean and cool, the way it always does out here in July when the Gulf Stream eddies and the cold pool underneath us keep doing their job. But there's a real story developing to our west: the cold wall that normally separates Block Island Sound from Rhode Island Sound has come apart — we're talking about a jump of better than ten degrees in RIS water temps over the last couple weeks. That's not a subtle shift. It means warm water that used to stay pinned east of Newport is now spreading, and it's already showing up in the bonito reports.

This week the moon swings new on the 11th, and that means building springs right through the weekend — bigger tidal exchange, stronger current at every rip and ledge from the Southwest Ledge to the Race. New moon springs are when Block Island does what it does best: it flushes bait hard through the rips and gives the bass something to lean into. I'd expect the bite to sharpen back up as the tidal push increases through Thursday and Friday, with the best window Saturday through Monday when the current's really moving and the fish stack up in the eddies behind the boulders. If you've fished the SW Ledge before you know the drill — anchor up-current of the structure, live-line an eel or drift back a chunk of fresh bunker, and let it swing into the wash. That's still the money program.

Bass fishing has actually been solid, not spectacular, but solid — and a couple of genuinely big fish have come off the Ledge and out around the North Rip in the last ten days, giants in the 30-to-40-pound class mixed in with a good number of schoolies and mid-20s fish. Eels are still king after dark, fished on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in 25 to 40 feet of water on the down-current side of the boulders. During the day, bucktails in the 2- to 4-ounce range tipped with a strip of squid have been drawing strikes when you can work them slow along the rock piles on the Ledge's western edge. Umbrella rigs trolled at 3 to 4 knots through the deeper water off the North Rip have also been putting bigger fish in the boat for guys willing to make the run out there and grind it out over a tide change.

Fluke have shifted, and this is worth knowing if you've been fishing the same spots with no results. The bay-side fluke bite has cooled off as inshore water has warmed into the high 70s, which pushed the better fish out to the channels, the inlets, and now into the ocean proper where upwelled water sitting around 71 degrees is holding bait tight to structure. Great Salt Pond's outflow and the deeper water off Old Harbor have both been producing keeper fluke on the outgoing tide — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom contours where the sand meets rock. Doesn't take much finesse, just patience and a slow drift. Some fish to 6 pounds have come out of that stretch in the last week, though it's not an every-drift bite — more like three or four keepers out of a full tide if you're covering ground.

Bluefish have been around but scattered — chopper-class fish mixed with smaller ones blitzing bait pods off Point Judith and along the Narragansett beaches, mostly at first light. Nothing sustained, but when you find the birds working you can load the boat fast on top-water plugs or tin.

The bonito news is the one to watch closest. With that cold wall gone soft between here and the mainland, the corridor that used to be strictly a Block Island phenomenon is stretching west toward Point Judith and Newport. I haven't seen numbers yet that make me want to plan a whole trip around it, but the water's right, and if the pattern holds through the weekend I'd expect the first real showing of bonito working bait schools off the Southwest Ledge and out toward the Newport Bridge area. Small metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Deadly Dicks — cast into diving birds is the move if you find them.

Looking ahead, the new moon springs building through the weekend are the whole story. Bigger current means bait gets pushed harder through the rips, and that's when the Ledge and the North Rip both wake up. If the wind stays out of the southwest and light like it's been, I'd plan to fish the last two hours of the outgoing tide Saturday and Sunday morning — that's where I'd put my money. Plan B if the bass don't cooperate is running the fluke drift off Old Harbor on that same tide. Either way, the water's healthy and the fish are here — the only question this week is timing it to the tide.
